question: A payments company runs its services on GKE. A recent audit found that an engineer had deployed a container image built on a laptop directly to the production cluster, bypassing the CI pipeline and vulnerability scanning. The company wants to guarantee that only images built by its Cloud Build pipeline and free of critical vulnerabilities can run in production, while keeping an audited emergency path. What should you do?
options: Restrict kubectl access to the production cluster to a single senior engineer who verifies image provenance manually before applying manifests

Enable Binary Authorization on the production cluster with a policy that requires attestations created by Cloud Build for provenance and by a vulnerability-scanning step for the absence of critical CVEs, configure dry-run mode first, and use break-glass annotations for audited emergency deployments
Configure a Kubernetes admission webhook that checks image names for the string 'cloudbuild' before admitting pods
Enable Artifact Analysis vulnerability scanning on Artifact Registry and send an email to the team whenever a critical vulnerability is found
explanation: Binary Authorization is the deploy-time policy control for GKE and Cloud Run: it admits only images that carry the required cryptographically signed attestations, such as a Cloud Build provenance attestation and a vulnerability-scan attestation, and it supports dry-run for safe rollout and break-glass annotations that allow but log emergency exceptions. Manual verification by one person (option A) is a bottleneck and not a reliable control. Matching image name strings (option C) is trivially spoofed and proves nothing about provenance. Scanning with email notifications (option D) provides visibility but does not prevent a vulnerable or unscanned image from being deployed.
hint: Core Rule: Binary Authorization is the deploy-time policy control for GKE and Cloud Run: it admits only images that carry the required cryptographically signed attestations, such as a Cloud Build provenance attestation and a vulnerability-scan attestation, and it supports dry-run for safe rollout and break-glass annotations that allow but log emergency exceptions.

question: A healthcare software vendor builds container images with Cloud Build and stores them in Artifact Registry. Vulnerability scanning is enabled on the registry, but images with critical CVEs still reach staging because the scan results are only reviewed weekly. The vendor wants the pipeline itself to block images that contain critical vulnerabilities before they are pushed or deployed. What should you do?
options: Add a Cloud Build step that runs Artifact Analysis On-Demand Scanning against the locally built image and fails the build when any vulnerability at or above the CRITICAL severity threshold is found, so that the image is never pushed
Create a log-based alert on Artifact Registry scan results and page the on-call engineer whenever a critical vulnerability is detected
Move image builds to developer laptops where engineers can inspect scan results before pushing

explanation: A quality gate must be enforced in the pipeline: On-Demand Scanning lets a Cloud Build step scan the image before it is pushed, and failing the build on critical findings guarantees vulnerable images never enter the registry or any environment. Alerting on registry scan results (option B) is reactive and does not stop the image from being deployed. Moving builds to laptops (option C) removes reproducibility and auditability and does not create an enforced gate. A more frequent manual review (option D) is still after the fact and relies on people.
hint: Core Rule (Security scanning gates in CI): A quality gate must be enforced in the pipeline: On-Demand Scanning lets a Cloud Build step scan the image before it is pushed, and failing the build on critical findings guarantees vulnerable images never enter the registry or any environment.

question: A ten-person startup pushes code directly to the main branch, and Cloud Build deploys every commit to production. Several recent outages were caused by simple mistakes that a second pair of eyes or a unit test would have caught. The team wants to add basic quality control with minimal process overhead. What should you do?
options: Introduce a weekly release meeting in which the CTO reviews every commit from the previous week before it is deployed
Require each developer to test changes manually in production behind an IP allowlist before merging
Protect the main branch so that changes arrive through pull requests that require at least one approving review and a passing Cloud Build presubmit run of the unit tests and linters before merge
Disable automatic deployment and have the on-call engineer deploy manually at the end of each day
explanation: Branch protection with mandatory peer review and an automated presubmit build is the lightweight, industry-standard quality gate: it catches mistakes before they merge, keeps continuous deployment intact, and scales with the team. A weekly CTO review (option A) delays every change by up to a week and creates a bottleneck. Manual testing in production (option B) exposes users to untested code and is not a repeatable control. Manual end-of-day deployment (option D) batches changes, which increases risk, and does not add any review or test.
hint: Core Rule (Code review and presubmit checks): Branch protection with mandatory peer review and an automated presubmit build is the lightweight, industry-standard quality gate: it catches mistakes before they merge, keeps continuous deployment intact, and scales with the team.

question: A media company's platform team is defining the mandatory quality gates that every service's Cloud Build pipeline must pass before an image can be promoted to the staging environment. They want gates that are objective, automated, and that measurably reduce defects reaching production. Which two gates should they require? (Choose two.)
options: Static analysis and linting of the source code, failing the build on high-severity findings such as hard-coded credentials or unsafe deserialization
A manual sign-off from the head of engineering recorded in an email thread
A requirement that the build finishes in under 60 seconds, to keep developers productive
Unit and integration test execution with a minimum code-coverage threshold that fails the build when coverage drops below the agreed level or when any test fails

A manual email sign-off (option B) is neither automated nor objective and adds latency. A build-duration limit (option C) is a productivity metric, not a quality gate, and could encourage skipping tests. Auto-merging based on tenure (option E) bypasses review entirely and is unrelated to code quality.

question: A retail bank manages all Google Cloud infrastructure with Terraform applied by Cloud Build. question: A telecommunications company operates 25 GKE clusters. Configuration is defined in a Git repository, but engineers frequently make emergency changes with kubectl edit that are never committed back, so clusters drift apart and later Git-based deployments overwrite fixes or fail unexpectedly. The company wants Git to be the enforced source of truth, wants drift to be corrected automatically, and wants to block resources that violate security policies at admission time. What should you do?
options: Run a nightly job that executes kubectl diff against every cluster and emails the differences to the platform team

Enable Config Sync on all clusters as part of a fleet, pointing at the Git repository, so that it continuously reconciles the declared state and reverts out-of-band changes, and enable Policy Controller with constraints that reject non-compliant resources at admission
Revoke kubectl access from all engineers and require every change, including emergencies, to go through a weekly change board
Use Cloud Deploy to redeploy all manifests to every cluster every hour so that manual changes are overwritten
explanation: Config Sync is GKE's GitOps controller: it continuously reconciles each cluster to the Git-declared state and automatically reverts drift caused by manual edits, and fleet-level management makes it uniform across all 25 clusters; Policy Controller adds admission-time enforcement of security and organizational constraints. A nightly diff email (option A) only reports drift, it does not correct or prevent it. Revoking all access with a weekly board (option C) makes emergency response impossible and does not address drift that already exists. Hourly redeploys with Cloud Deploy (option D) is a blunt, resource-intensive workaround that neither detects drift promptly nor enforces policy.
hint: Core Rule (Configuration drift on GKE): Config Sync is GKE's GitOps controller: it continuously reconciles each cluster to the Git-declared state and automatically reverts drift caused by manual edits, and fleet-level management makes it uniform across all 25 clusters; Policy Controller adds admission-time enforcement of security and organizational constraints.

question: A logistics company provisions all Compute Engine, Cloud SQL, and networking resources with Terraform. During a recent incident, engineers discovered that a firewall rule had been modified in the console months earlier and that the Terraform state no longer matched reality, which caused a later apply to unexpectedly remove the change. The company wants to detect such drift within a day and reduce the chance that it happens again. What should you recommend?
options: Schedule a daily Cloud Build job that runs terraform plan against production and raises an alert or ticket when the plan is not empty, and remove direct console and gcloud modification permissions from engineers so that changes must flow through the pipeline

Audit logs (option C) record who changed what, but weekly manual review is slow and does not compare against the desired state. State versioning (option D) protects the state file itself but does nothing to detect that reality has diverged from it.
hint: Core Rule (Infrastructure drift detection): Drift detection for Terraform-managed infrastructure is achieved by regularly executing a plan against live state and surfacing any difference; combining that with least-privilege IAM that removes out-of-band write access closes the gap that allowed the manual edit.

question: A ticketing platform's search service has an availability SLO of 99.9%. For the last four quarters it has actually delivered 99.99%, user satisfaction scores are high, and the team has never come close to exhausting its error budget. At the quarterly SLO review, one engineer proposes raising the SLO to 99.99% because 'that is what we deliver anyway'. What should you advise?
options: Raise the SLO to 99.99% immediately, because an SLO should always reflect the best performance the service has demonstrated
Remove the SLO, since the service is clearly reliable enough and the objective is no longer useful
Raise the SLO to 99.999% to give the team an ambitious target for next year

Keep the SLO at 99.9% unless users actually need more reliability; instead, use the unspent error budget deliberately, for example to increase release velocity, run chaos experiments, or perform risky upgrades, and confirm that the SLI still reflects the user experience
explanation: An SLO should represent the reliability users need, not the maximum the system has happened to achieve; tightening it merely because performance exceeded it would raise costs and constrain future change without a user benefit, and it removes the room to spend budget on innovation and resilience testing that SRE recommends. Raising the SLO reflexively (options A and C) creates an ever-tightening trap and makes every future change riskier. Deleting the SLO (option B) removes the shared language between product and engineering and the alerting that protects users. Periodic SLO reviews should ask whether the SLI and target still match user happiness, which is what the correct option does.
hint: Core Rule (SLO reviews): An SLO should represent the reliability users need, not the maximum the system has happened to achieve; tightening it merely because performance exceeded it would raise costs and constrain future change without a user benefit, and it removes the room to spend budget on innovation and resilience testing that SRE recommends.

question: An online brokerage runs its trading API on a regional managed instance group distributed evenly across three zones, with the autoscaler targeting 90% CPU utilization to minimize cost. During a recent zonal disruption, the surviving instances in the other two zones were immediately overloaded and the API returned errors for 20 minutes until the autoscaler added capacity. The business wants the API to survive the loss of any single zone without user impact. What should you recommend?
options: Lower the autoscaler's target utilization so that steady-state load per zone leaves enough headroom for the remaining zones to absorb a failed zone's traffic (roughly no more than two-thirds utilization with three zones), and verify with a game day that simulates zone loss
Move the instance group to a single zone with larger machine types so that a zonal outage affects either all traffic or none, simplifying the failure mode

A single zone (option B) eliminates zonal resilience entirely. Zero cool-down (option C) does not solve instance boot time and can cause oscillation. Unmanaged groups (option D) lose autoscaling and autohealing and rely on humans during the worst moments.

question: A fintech company must perform an annual third-party penetration test of its customer-facing application, which runs on GKE, Cloud Run, and Cloud SQL, to satisfy PCI DSS. question: A ticket-sales platform is launching sales for a major concert tour and expects a sudden spike to 50,000 requests per second within a minute of the on-sale time. The team's current load test runs a single script from one engineer's laptop against staging at 500 requests per second and passes. The architect is asked whether the platform is ready. Which testing approach should you recommend before the sale?
options: Approve the launch, because the platform is serverless and will scale automatically to whatever traffic arrives
Run the existing laptop test for a longer duration, since duration matters more than throughput for finding problems

Assuming serverless scaling suffices (option A) ignores cold starts, per-region limits, and non-elastic dependencies. Longer duration at trivial throughput (option B) misses the spike behavior entirely. Mocking the back end (option C) hides exactly the components most likely to fail under load.
